deed: Jonas Salk gave the polio vaccine to the world without a patent and without profit
title: Jonas Salk, from a family of Jewish immigrants, developed the polio vaccine and gave it to the world without a patent

trailer.text: Jonas Salk was a medical researcher who, with his staff, developed the first successful vaccine against polio, and because of it he became an international hero.
Jonas Salk was born in New York in 1914; according to the Salk Institute his parents were Russian-Jewish immigrants, while the Whonamedit dictionary says they came from Poland.
In 1947 he moved to direct the Virus Research Laboratory at the University of Pittsburgh, and there he and his staff developed a vaccine against polio.
On 12 April 1955 Thomas Francis announced that Salk's vaccine was up to 90% effective in preventing paralytic polio.
When asked on television who owned the patent on the vaccine, Salk replied that it belonged to the people and that one could not patent the sun.

stations.title: A child of immigrants in New York

paragraphs.text: Jonas Salk was born on 28 October 1914 in New York.
He was the oldest of three sons of Daniel Salk and Dora Press.
He grew up in East Harlem in Manhattan and in the Crotona section of the Bronx.
According to the Whonamedit dictionary, his parents were Ashkenazi Jewish immigrants from Poland.
According to The Forward, his parents had little formal education, and they wanted to see their children succeed.
After his internship, Salk had difficulty finding a suitable residency or research fellowship.
One of the reasons was the anti-Semitism that pervaded many medical and scientific centers.
According to Mental Floss, several labs rejected him, perhaps due to quotas that discriminated against Jews.
According to the Salk Institute, Jonas Salk was born to Russian-Jewish immigrants Daniel and Dora Salk.
In 1952, 57,628 polio cases were reported in the United States.
It was the worst polio epidemic on record in the United States.
According to Whonamedit, of nearly 58,000 cases reported, 3,145 people died and 21,269 were left with paralysis of varying degrees, from mild to disabling.
According to Peter Salk, his son, around 58,000 American children contracted polio that year.
Fewer than ten percent of those who fell ill died.
But many more were paralyzed: they could not move their arms and legs, or breathe without the help of machines.
As early as the 1930s, two attempts to create a vaccine that would produce immunity had failed.
In 1947 Salk moved to direct the Virus Research Laboratory at the University of Pittsburgh.
According to his son Peter, he set up his own lab there and gathered a strong team to work on a polio vaccine.
According to Peter, his father was working on a vaccine that could prevent polio epidemics entirely.
In 1949 Enders, Robbins and Weller developed a way to grow poliovirus in tissue culture.
It was a breakthrough that aided in the creation of the vaccine.
Elsie Ward and Julius Youngner of Salk's team came up with a quick way to check whether live polioviruses remained in samples.
According to the Jewish Journal, Salk went against the scientific consensus that only live viruses could produce an effective vaccine.
On 2 July 1952 Salk injected 43 children with the killed-virus vaccine, assisted by the staff of the Watson Home for Crippled Children.
According to NPR's timeline, nearly 15,000 subjects in the Pittsburgh area, mostly children, received the vaccine in pilot trials.
Salk announced that his wife and three sons had been among the first volunteers to be inoculated.
According to Peter, his father brought vaccine home, boiled the syringes and needles on the stove, and vaccinated his children.
By 1953, after a summer with 58,000 polio cases, the director of the National Foundation agreed to invest millions of dollars in producing and testing the vaccine.
The trials and the evaluation were funded by grants totalling $7,500,000 from the funds of the March of Dimes fundraising campaign of the National Foundation for Infantile Paralysis.
According to Peter Salk, a hundred million Americans contributed to the effort.
Between April and July 1954 more than 1.8 million schoolchildren took part in the national field trial.
The children came from the United States, Canada and Finland, and trials of this scope were unprecedented.
In one trial, half of the children received the vaccine and the other half a placebo.
No doctor or family knew who received what.
According to the encyclopedia, the children were joined by some 20,000 doctors, 40,000 nurses, 14,000 school principals, 50,000 teachers and 200,000 volunteers.
On 12 April 1955 Salk returned with his family to Ann Arbor, for a large public meeting at which the results were announced.
Thomas Francis announced that the vaccine was up to 90% effective in preventing paralytic polio.
In the placebo areas, 33 inoculated children became paralyzed, compared with 115 uninoculated children.
Of 233 inoculated children exposed to polio in the family, only one developed the disease, compared with 8 of 244 children who received placebo.
According to the encyclopedia, on that day Salk became an international hero.
The vaccine was immediately licensed for commercial distribution by the Department of Health, Education, and Welfare.
The March of Dimes spent $9 million to ensure an adequate supply of vaccine in the days after the announcement.
According to The Forward, 12 April 1955 almost became a national holiday.
Salk was invited to the White House.
There President Eisenhower publicly thanked him, on behalf of the parents and grandparents of the world.
In a television interview, Edward Murrow asked Salk who owned the patent on the vaccine.
Salk replied that the patent belonged to the people, and that one could not patent the sun.
According to a Retro Report film, Salk publicly opposed the idea of patenting the discovery and profiting from it.
According to his son Peter, Salk saw this as a natural evolution of science, and the results belong to the people.
According to Whonamedit, Salk's sole aim was to develop a safe and effective vaccine as rapidly as possible, with no interest in personal profit.
According to the Jewish Journal, by declining to patent, Salk effectively turned down a fortune.
According to a Forbes estimate, had he owned the patent, he could have earned $7 billion.
According to Brian Palmer, there was a consensus within the organization that the public had already paid for the vaccine through its donations, and a for-profit patent would be double charging.
According to Palmer, the organization had already committed to give the vaccine formulation and production processes to several pharmaceutical companies for free.
According to Robert Cook-Deegan, the National Foundation was a centralized, nonprofit research and development operation.
According to Marcia Angell, in those days some scientists held that you could either do well or do good, but it was hard to do both.
According to Peter Salk, within seven years the incidence of polio in the United States dropped by 97 percent.
Albert Sabin later developed a live-virus vaccine given by mouth.
In January 2000 the CDC recommended that use of the oral vaccine be phased out.
In 1956 Salk won the Lasker Award, and he advocated mandatory vaccination.
In 1977 he was awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom.
The Salk Institute was founded in 1960 and formally opened in 1963, financed largely by the March of Dimes.
Later in life Salk wanted to develop an AIDS vaccine.
A venture capitalist approached him and asked him to form a biotech company.
In 1986 Salk cofounded the Immune Response Corporation, for a novel approach to managing AIDS.
He died on 23 June 1995 in La Jolla, California.
A production error at Cutter Laboratories left live virus in some of the vaccine.
The error caused 204 cases of vaccine-associated polio and eleven deaths.
Albert Sabin, Salk's main scientific rival, worked tirelessly in the early 1950s to postpone and discredit the field trial of the Salk vaccine.
Sabin later joined the committee that recommended licensing.
According to Mental Floss, Sabin called Salk a "kitchen chemist" and tried to discredit the use of a killed virus.
According to Mental Floss, other scientists resented Salk for succeeding outside the medical establishment and for getting all the accolades.
According to NPR, Youngner, then 84, said Salk offended some of his colleagues by refusing to credit their contributions to the development of the vaccine.
Salk was never elected to the National Academy of Sciences or awarded the Nobel Prize, two honors that were much discussed in the triumphant period after 1955.
The patent story is also disputed.

According to Palmer, the Foundation's attorneys examined a possible patent before the interview and concluded that the vaccine did not meet the novelty requirement and that the application would fail.
Palmer called Salk's response to Murrow a "dangerous intuition pump".
According to Mental Floss, some scholars criticize Salk for presenting himself as an altruist.
According to Palmer, Salk's company moved to patent the AIDS vaccine in the project's early days.

disagreements.question: How many children were actually vaccinated in the field trial?

versions.says: The encyclopedia: almost 450,000 children in the first to third grades
Brian Palmer: more than 650,000 children
The Forward: over 600,000 schoolchildren injected with the vaccine or a placebo, and a million more served as a control group

disagreements.question: How many people, besides the children, helped organize the trial?

versions.says: Whonamedit: 20,000 physicians and public health officers, 64,000 school personnel and 220,000 volunteers
The encyclopedia: some 20,000 doctors, 40,000 nurses, 14,000 school principals, 50,000 teachers and 200,000 volunteers

disagreements.question: How many people contributed to the effort against polio?

versions.says: Peter Salk: a hundred million Americans
Brian Palmer: 80 million people in the year the vaccine was unveiled

disagreements.question: In what year was the Sabin vaccine developed or introduced?

versions.says: NPR: in 1961, an oral vaccine
Whonamedit: in 1960, a live-virus vaccine
Mental Floss: in 1962, an oral vaccine on a sugar cube

disagreements.question: How many polio cases were there in the United States per year before the vaccine?

versions.says: NPR: some 20,000 cases a year in the early 1950s
The Forward: between 25,000 and 50,000 new cases a year in the 1950s
Brian Palmer: between 13,000 and 20,000 children paralyzed a year
Thomas Francis in the announcement: up to 90% in preventing paralytic polio
The University of Michigan press release: up to 80-90 percent in preventing paralytic polio

disagreements.question: By how much did polio cases drop after the vaccine?

versions.says: Peter Salk: a drop of 97 percent within seven years
NPR: a drop of 85-90 percent in U.S. polio cases in 1955–1957.
NPR: from some 20,000 cases a year in the early 1950s to about 3,000 a year by 1960

disagreements.question: Where did Salk's parents emigrate from?

versions.says: Salk Institute: Russian-Jewish immigrants
Whonamedit: Ashkenazi Jewish immigrants from Poland
Mental Floss: his mother Dora left Russia in 1901; his father Daniel was the son of immigrants from Eastern Europe

disagreements.question: Where did Salk's parents emigrate from?

versions.says: Salk Institute: Russian-Jewish immigrants

disagreements.question: Was Salk's father himself an immigrant?

versions.says: Salk Institute: both parents, Daniel and Dora, were Russian-Jewish immigrants
Mental Floss: his father Daniel was the son of Jewish immigrants from Eastern Europe; his mother Dora emigrated from Russia
